metadata.title: Muse vs Codex vs Gemini: The Indie Artist's Stack
metadata.note: Slate cut per Bear's 2026-10-04 standing rule. No single article compares these tools; the comparison frame comes from the mission brief (Muse, Codex, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Gemini) and the article's thesis that tools are neutral and intent decides. Tool descriptions kept structural, never pricing or version claims. Numbers written as words for Kokoro; no raw digits in narration.

beats.narration_text: Every week, a new announcement. A new model. A new game-changer that will revolutionize your music career. You are an indie artist with songs to finish, and your feed is a slot machine of AI tools. Here is the truth nobody selling you a tool will say out loud: the tool is not the point.

shot.title: The tool slot machine
shot.dek: The tool is not the point.

beats.narration_text: Muse versus Codex versus Gemini. Claude Code versus Claude Cowork. The internet wants this to be a cage match with one winner. It is not. It is a toolbox. You do not ask which is better, the hammer or the saw. You ask which job each one does. This is your stack.

shot.title: The pitch
shot.dek: A toolbox, not a cage match.

beats.narration_text: There is a special circle of hell reserved for the artist who spends the evening comparing AI tools instead of making music. The paradox of choice: the more options on the shelf, the less gets made. Endless tool comparison is procrastination wearing a lab coat.

shot.title: The paradox of choice
shot.dek: Comparing tools is procrastination in a lab coat.

beats.narration_text: So let us skip the feature matrix. It rots in a quarter. Prices change, models merge, the best this spring is a footnote by fall. What does not rot is the shape of the work. Every one of these tools is one of three animals: a talker, a coder, or a fetcher. Learn the animals, not the brand names.

shot.title: Skip the feature matrix
shot.dek: Learn the animals, not the brand names.

beats.narration_text: The talkers: Muse, Gemini, Claude. You converse with them. They draft your bio, your press release, your grant application, your between-songs banter. They brainstorm a hundred merch ideas before breakfast, then argue with you about the weak ones. If the job is words, give it to a talker.

shot.title: The talkers
shot.dek: If the job is words, give it to a talker.

beats.narration_text: The coders: Claude Code, Codex. They do not chat about your website. They open it. They edit the files, run the build, fix the thing that broke at midnight before release day. Your promo site, your mailing list script, the merch page that never quite worked on phones. If the job lives in files, give it to a coder.

shot.title: The coders
shot.dek: If the job lives in files, give it to a coder.

beats.narration_text: The fetchers: the research side of all of them. They go out and come back carrying things. Playlist curator contacts. Grant deadlines. What venues pay in your city, and which distributors take what cut. You used to spend a whole Tuesday doing this. Now you spend the Tuesday checking their work.

shot.title: The fetchers
shot.dek: Spend Tuesday checking their work, not doing it.

beats.narration_text: Rule one: one job, one tool. Do not ask the talker to rewrite your website code. Do not ask the coder to write your artist bio. Every tool fails most embarrassingly outside its shape. The stack works when each animal stays in its lane.

shot.title: Rule one: one job, one tool
shot.dek: Each animal stays in its lane.

beats.narration_text: Rule two: you are the intent. The same tools, pointed differently — that is the whole game. A talker in the hands of an artist with something to say writes a manifesto. In the hands of someone with nothing to say, it writes sludge. The difference was never the tool. It is who is pointing it, and at what.

shot.title: Rule two: you are the intent
shot.dek: The difference was never the tool.

beats.narration_text: Start free. Every one of these tools has a free tier, and the free tier is a complete education. Pay only when a tool has earned its keep — when you can point to the release, the site, the grant that would not exist without it. Subscriptions are for tools with a track record, not tools with a landing page.

shot.title: Start free
shot.dek: Subscriptions are for tools with a track record.

beats.narration_text: Picture a release week. Monday: the talker drafts the announcement, the one-sheet, the pitch emails. Tuesday: the coder ships the pre-save page and fixes the mailing list form. Wednesday: the fetcher brings you fifty playlist curators who actually cover your genre. Thursday: you, the human, listen to everything and cut what is weak. Friday: release.

shot.title: A release week, stacked
shot.dek: Thursday: you listen, and cut what is weak.

beats.narration_text: What you do not stack: the parts that need you. Your taste. Your ear. The decision that the bridge is wrong. No tool gets a vote on the music itself. The stack handles the everything-around-the-music, so your hours go to the music. That is the entire economics of it.

shot.title: What you do not stack
shot.dek: No tool gets a vote on the music.

beats.narration_text: One honest warning: this film has an expiry date. The tools will merge, rename, and relaunch. The stack I just described will look quaint. So do not marry a tool. Marry the habit: every few months, spend one afternoon re-testing the shelf. The winners are not the artists with the perfect stack. They are the ones who re-stack.

shot.title: The rot problem
shot.dek: Do not marry a tool. Marry the habit.

beats.narration_text: Here is your unfair advantage. A major label needs six meetings and a procurement process to adopt a new tool. You need an afternoon. You are the entire IT department, and the IT department says yes. Speed of adoption is the one game the indie artist can win outright. Play it.

shot.title: The indie advantage
shot.dek: You are the entire IT department, and it says yes.

beats.narration_text: So: Muse versus Codex versus Gemini. The answer is yes. Talkers for words, coders for files, fetchers for legwork. Three tools, learned deep, pointed with intent. The stack should be boring. Boring tools, interesting artist. That is the whole philosophy.

Pick three. Learn them like instruments, not like apps. Practice until the tool disappears and only the work is left. Then go make the thing no tool can make for you: the song. The stack is ready when you are.

shot.title: Outro
shot.dek: Pick three. Then make the thing no tool can make.
